questiontext.text: What is the core greedy strategy of Kruskal's minimum spanning tree algorithm?

answer.text: Sort all edges by weight, then add the next-smallest edge that does not form a cycle

feedback.text: Correct — Kruskal grows a forest by adding safe, globally cheapest edges.

answer.text: Grow one tree from a start vertex by adding the cheapest crossing edge

feedback.text: That is Prim's algorithm, not Kruskal's.

answer.text: Let every component pick its cheapest outgoing edge each round

feedback.text: That is Borůvka's algorithm.

answer.text: Explore depth-first and keep the first spanning tree found

feedback.text: DFS builds a spanning tree but ignores weights, so it is not minimum.

generalfeedback.text: Kruskal considers edges in nondecreasing weight order and accepts each one unless it would connect two vertices already in the same component.

questiontext.text: Which data structure does Kruskal use to test efficiently whether adding an edge would create a cycle?

feedback.text: Correct — find checks if endpoints share a set; union merges them.
That is Prim's tool; Kruskal sorts edges and uses union-find.
A queue is for BFS traversal, not cycle testing in Kruskal.

answer.text: A balanced binary search tree of edge weights

feedback.text: Sorting handles weights; cycle testing needs union-find.

generalfeedback.text: Union-find gives near-constant amortized find/union, so each cycle test when adding an edge is very cheap.

questiontext.text: What dominates the running time of Kruskal's algorithm on a graph with E edges?

answer.text: O(E log E) — dominated by sorting the edges

feedback.text: Correct — the sort dominates; union-find operations are nearly linear.

answer.text: O(V^2) from scanning a matrix each step

feedback.text: That is a dense-Prim bound, not Kruskal's.

answer.text: O(V!) from trying all spanning trees

feedback.text: Kruskal is greedy and polynomial, not brute force.

answer.text: O(E) with no sorting at all

feedback.text: Kruskal must order edges by weight, so sorting cost applies.

generalfeedback.text: Sorting the E edges costs O(E log E); the subsequent union-find work is almost linear, so the sort dominates.

questiontext.text: For which kind of graph is Kruskal's algorithm often a particularly good fit?

answer.text: Sparse graphs, where E is small relative to V^2

feedback.text: Correct — few edges keep the dominant edge-sort cheap.
Kruskal works on any connected weighted graph and shines on sparse ones.
MST algorithms need edge weights; unweighted MST is trivial.
MSTs are defined on undirected weighted graphs.

generalfeedback.text: Because Kruskal's cost is driven by sorting E edges, it is attractive when E is small — that is, on sparse graphs.

questiontext.text: Kruskal's algorithm considers edges in nondecreasing order of weight.

feedback.text: Correct — it processes the smallest available edge first.
Sorting edges from smallest to largest is central to Kruskal.

questiontext.text: Kruskal adds an edge even when both of its endpoints are already in the same connected component.

feedback.text: No — that edge would form a cycle, so Kruskal rejects it.
Correct — an edge whose endpoints share a component is skipped to avoid a cycle.

questiontext.text: Kruskal tests for cycles using a disjoint-set structure also known by the hyphenated English name ______ (e.g. "union-find").

feedback.text: Correct — the disjoint-set / union-find structure.
Correct.
Correct — also called a disjoint-set structure.

questiontext.text: Which statements about Kruskal's algorithm are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It is a greedy algorithm that adds globally cheapest safe edges

feedback.text: Yes — it always takes the smallest edge that avoids a cycle.

answer.text: Its running time is dominated by sorting the edges, O(E log E)

feedback.text: Yes — sorting is the bottleneck.

answer.text: It uses a min-priority queue to grow a single tree from a start vertex

feedback.text: No — that is Prim's approach, not Kruskal's.
No — Kruskal sorts by weight; weights are essential.

generalfeedback.text: Kruskal is a greedy, sort-then-union-find algorithm running in O(E log E); it grows a forest by weight order, unlike Prim's single-tree priority-queue growth.
